title: Scripture alone — or scripture read within tradition?
question: Where does final authority for Christian faith and practice lie: in the Bible read by each believer, in the Bible as the sole infallible rule read within the church's creedal heritage, or in scripture and tradition together as interpreted by the church's teaching office?
intro:
Every Christian tradition reveres scripture. The disagreement is about how scripture relates to the church that received, copied, canonized and interpreted it. Three broad answers are compared here. Biblicism (sometimes called 'solo scriptura' by its critics) holds that the individual believer, reading the Bible directly, needs no creed or tradition as an authority alongside it. Sola scriptura, as the sixteenth-century magisterial Reformers framed it, holds that scripture is the only infallible rule, but that it is rightly read within the church and with the help of the ecumenical creeds as subordinate, fallible standards. The Catholic and Orthodox position holds that God's revelation is handed on through both scripture and holy tradition, and that the church (in Catholic teaching, the bishops in communion with the pope; in Orthodox teaching, the conciliar mind of the church) authentically interprets it.

The questions underneath are concrete: who settled the canon; whether the New Testament itself points to oral traditions; how disagreements among Bible readers are to be resolved; and whether any church body can be preserved from error. Each view has a long pedigree and serious defenders, and each has a characteristic weakness its rivals press.

positions.name: Biblicism (no creed but the Bible)
positions.summary:
Biblicism holds that the Bible alone, read directly by ordinary believers, is sufficient for faith and practice, and that creeds, confessions and church traditions have no binding authority at all. In its classic American Restorationist form (the Stone-Campbell movement), the slogan 'no creed but the Bible' expressed the hope that if Christians dropped human formulations and returned to the plain New Testament pattern, sectarian division would end and the primitive church would be restored.

Biblicists do not usually deny that history, scholarship or teachers can help; they deny that any of these has authority to bind conscience or to settle what the Bible means. The individual reader, guided by the Spirit and using common sense, stands directly before the text. Critics, notably Keith Mathison, call this 'solo scriptura' to distinguish it from the Reformers' sola scriptura.

figures.name: Thomas Campbell
figures.bio: An Irish Seceder Presbyterian who emigrated to western Pennsylvania in 1807. Censured by his presbytery for serving communion to Presbyterians outside his own branch, he formed the Christian Association of Washington and wrote its founding document, arguing that Christian unity should rest only on what the New Testament expressly teaches, not on inferences or creeds.

works.author: Thomas Campbell
works.title: Declaration and Address of the Christian Association of Washington

figures.name: Alexander Campbell
figures.profession: Preacher, editor, debater, founder of Bethany College
figures.bio: Thomas Campbell's son became the leading theologian of the Disciples of Christ. Through his periodicals and public debates he argued that creeds were the chief cause of division, that the New Testament gives a recoverable pattern for worship and church order, and that scripture interpreted by sound reason using ordinary rules of language needs no confessional supplement.

figures.name: Barton W. Stone
figures.bio: A leader at the Cane Ridge revival in Kentucky (1801). He and colleagues dissolved their Springfield Presbytery in 1804, declaring a wish to 'sink into union with the body of Christ' and to take the Bible as the only sure guide. His 'Christians' merged with Campbell's 'Disciples' in 1832.

works.author: Barton W. Stone and others
works.title: The Last Will and Testament of the Springfield Presbytery

figures.name: James O'Kelly
figures.bio: Broke with Francis Asbury's Methodist episcopacy in 1792 and led the Republican Methodists, who soon called themselves simply 'Christians' and took the Bible as their only creed. His movement is often counted among the independent streams that fed American Restorationism.

works.title: The Author's Apology for Protesting Against the Methodist Episcopal Government

positions.context:
Biblicism flourished in the early American republic. Nathan Hatch has shown how revolutionary ideals of liberty, suspicion of clerical elites and confidence in the common person shaped popular religion: ordinary people were told they could read the Bible for themselves and should not submit to inherited authorities. Scottish Common Sense philosophy supplied an epistemology in which a plain text, read by a sincere mind, yields its meaning.

The movement produced the Churches of Christ, the Christian Churches and the Disciples of Christ, and its instincts spread widely in nondenominational evangelicalism. Ironically, the hope of unity was followed by further divisions (for example over instrumental music and missionary societies), which critics treat as a test case of the method.
claims: Scripture is the only authority that binds the conscience; creeds, confessions and councils have no authority over a believer.
The Bible is clear enough on everything necessary that an ordinary sincere reader can understand it without an official interpreter.
Human creeds have historically caused division by imposing inferences as tests of fellowship.
The New Testament supplies a pattern for the church's faith, worship and order that can and should be restored.
Where scripture speaks Christians should speak, and where it is silent they should be silent.
Each believer is personally responsible before God to test all teaching by scripture.

scriptures.reading: The Bereans are praised for checking even an apostle's preaching against the scriptures for themselves; every believer should do the same with every teacher.
Jesus condemns traditions that nullify God's word; creeds and church traditions are human traditions of exactly this kind when imposed as authorities.
Scripture is God-breathed and makes the believer complete and equipped for every good work; nothing else is needed.
Christians are not to call any human teacher master; all are siblings under one teacher, Christ.
The anointing of the Spirit teaches believers, so they do not depend on human teachers to know the truth.
Nothing may be added to or taken from God's commands; binding creeds add human words to God's.
The closing warning against adding to the prophecy expresses the principle that the written word is complete.
Jesus prays for the unity of all believers; unity on the Bible alone, rather than on competing creeds, is the path to answering that prayer.

arguments.text: The New Testament repeatedly tells believers to test teachers by the word, never the reverse; no text appoints a later body to bind interpretation.
Jesus' critique of the Pharisees shows that religious tradition, even well-meant, can come to override scripture; the safest course is to treat no tradition as authoritative.
If a creed is true it adds nothing to scripture, and if it is false it should not be held; either way it should not be a test of fellowship.
Any interpreting authority must itself be interpreted; making the Bible the only authority avoids an infinite regress of interpreters.
Denominational lines in the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries were drawn largely along confessional boundaries; abandoning creeds was a serious attempt to heal those divisions.

Medieval accretions such as indulgences grew under the shelter of tradition; the Reformers' own churches later hardened into new confessional orthodoxies, suggesting that any tradition-based authority drifts.

critiques.text: Keith Mathison argues that this is 'solo scriptura', a departure from the Reformation. By making each individual the final judge of what scripture means, it does not eliminate tradition but replaces the church's tradition with the reader's private one, and it cannot adjudicate between rival readings except by majority or personality.

Christian Smith's *The Bible Made Impossible* (2011) argues that biblicism generates 'pervasive interpretive pluralism': sincere, competent Bible readers who share biblicist assumptions reach many incompatible conclusions, which undercuts the claim that the Bible is clear and self-sufficient in the way biblicism requires. Catholic and Orthodox critics add that the Bible never claims to be the only authority, and that the canon itself was recognized by the church.
Historically, the Restorationist ideal of no creed produced new divisions within a generation, which suggests that rejecting creeds does not deliver the promised unity.

responses.text: Defenders reply that 'solo' is a caricature: Campbell valued learning, history and reasoned debate. The point is not that every reader is infallible but that no reader's conclusions, including a council's, may bind another's conscience. Mistakes are corrected by better exegesis, which is equally the remedy within confessional churches.

Responses to Smith, such as Kevin DeYoung's 2011 review, argue that he exaggerates the range and depth of evangelical disagreement, that there is wide agreement on central matters, and that disagreement among readers reflects human limitation rather than a defect in scripture. Biblicists add that Catholic and Orthodox readers also disagree, so an authoritative interpreter does not remove pluralism; it relocates it.

Later divisions came, defenders say, when the movement's own conventions hardened into unwritten creeds; the remedy is more consistent application of the principle, not its abandonment. The movement also produced remarkable cooperation across former denominational lines.

strawMen.strawMan: Biblicists think they read the Bible with no assumptions at all.
strawMen.correction: Thoughtful Restorationists acknowledged rules of interpretation (Campbell wrote about them at length); their claim is about authority, not about having no method.

strawMen.strawMan: Biblicism rejects all teachers, scholarship and history.
strawMen.correction: The movement founded colleges and valued learning. It rejects binding authority for these, not their usefulness.

strawMen.strawMan: Biblicism is the same as the Reformers' sola scriptura.
strawMen.correction: Many Protestants, notably Mathison, insist the two differ: the Reformers affirmed creeds and church authority as real though subordinate, which biblicism denies.

positive: Encouraged ordinary believers to read and know the Bible for themselves.
Gave a strong check against clerical manipulation and unexamined custom.
Fueled serious, if imperfect, efforts toward Christian unity across denominational lines.
Produced vigorous traditions of congregational Bible study and lay leadership.
negative: Left no agreed way to settle interpretive disputes, contributing to fragmentation.
Tended to underrate the creeds' role in guarding Trinitarian and Christological doctrine.
Could mask a reader's own cultural assumptions behind a claim to read the 'plain' text.
Detached many believers from the wisdom of earlier centuries.

adherents: Some Baptist and Pentecostal congregations in practice

positions.name: Sola scriptura (Reformational)
positions.summary:
The magisterial Reformers (Luther, Zwingli, Calvin, Cranmer and their heirs) taught that scripture is the only infallible rule of faith and the final court of appeal, because it alone is God's own word. They did not reject tradition as such. They received the ecumenical creeds, read the church fathers carefully, wrote confessions, and expected scripture to be read in the communion of the church under ordained teachers. Tradition, councils and confessions are real authorities, but secondary and fallible ones, always open to correction by scripture.

Keith Mathison's *The Shape of Sola Scriptura* (2001) recast this as the difference between 'Tradition 1' (a single source of revelation, scripture, interpreted within the church's rule of faith) and 'Tradition 2' (two sources, scripture plus unwritten tradition), terms he borrowed from Heiko Oberman. On this account the Reformers sought to recover the early church's Tradition 1 position against both late-medieval Tradition 2 and radical individualism.

figures.name: Martin Luther
figures.profession: Augustinian friar, professor of Bible at Wittenberg
figures.bio: At the Leipzig Disputation (1519) Luther conceded that popes and councils had erred, and at the Diet of Worms (1521) he refused to recant unless convinced by scripture and plain reason, since his conscience was captive to the word of God. He nonetheless retained the creeds, much liturgy, and infant baptism, and strongly opposed radicals who set private inspiration against the external word.

works.title: To the Christian Nobility of the German Nation

works.author: Martin Luther
works.title: On the Councils and the Church

figures.name: John Calvin
figures.bio: Calvin argued that scripture is self-authenticating, its authority confirmed by the inner witness of the Spirit rather than conferred by the church. He also treated the early councils with great respect, citing Nicaea, Constantinople, Ephesus and Chalcedon as faithful expositions of scripture whose authority rests on their agreement with it.

figures.name: Martin Chemnitz
figures.bio: Chemnitz wrote the most thorough Protestant reply to the Council of Trent. He distinguished several senses of 'tradition', accepting those that hand on and faithfully interpret scripture, and rejecting the claim that unwritten traditions carry doctrines not found in scripture.

works.author: Martin Chemnitz
works.title: Examination of the Council of Trent

figures.name: Westminster Assembly
figures.profession: Assembly of English and Scottish divines
figures.bio: The Westminster Confession states that the whole counsel of God is either expressly set down in scripture or deduced from it by good and necessary consequence, that the Spirit speaking in scripture is the supreme judge of controversies, and that synods and councils may err and are to be used as a help, not a rule.

figures.name: Keith A. Mathison
figures.profession: Reformed theologian, professor at Reformation Bible College
figures.bio: Mathison's 2001 book argued that much modern evangelicalism had drifted into 'solo scriptura', and that the Reformation doctrine, rightly understood, places scripture as sole infallible authority within the church and the hermeneutical context of the ancient rule of faith.

positions.context:
In the late medieval church, theologians debated whether all saving truth was contained in scripture (with tradition as its interpretation) or whether some truths came through an unwritten apostolic tradition. Heiko Oberman labeled these Tradition 1 and Tradition 2. Indulgence controversies and appeals to papal authority brought the question to a head in 1517–1521. When Luther appealed to scripture over pope and council, he was pressed to say who decides what scripture means; his answer was that scripture interprets itself, clear passages illuminating obscure ones.

The Reformers fought on two fronts: against Rome's claim that the church's teaching office stands with scripture as an authority, and against Anabaptist and spiritualist radicals whom they accused of individualism and private revelation. Lutheran, Reformed and Anglican confessions all retained the Apostles', Nicene and Athanasian Creeds.
claims: Scripture is the only infallible and final authority for faith and life.
Scripture is sufficient: everything necessary for salvation and godliness is taught in it explicitly or by necessary inference.
Scripture is clear in what is necessary for salvation, so that ordinary believers can grasp it with ordinary means.
Creeds, councils and confessions are genuine but subordinate authorities, binding only insofar as they agree with scripture.
Scripture is to be read in the church, under its ministry, and in continuity with the ancient rule of faith.
The church recognizes the canon; it does not create its authority.
Any church body, however venerable, can err and must be corrected by scripture.

scriptures.reading: Only scripture is described as God-breathed; it makes the man of God complete, implying material sufficiency for doctrine and life.
Jesus judges the elders' tradition by the written word; tradition is legitimate only when it submits to scripture.
Teaching must be tested 'to the law and to the testimony'; the written word is the standard.
The Jerusalem council is a model of synodical authority: it deliberates, appeals to scripture (Amos 9), and issues decisions, yet its authority is ministerial under the word.
Even an apostle or an angel is to be rejected if he preaches a different gospel; the message, now written, stands above every messenger.
Paul's traditions were delivered orally and by letter while apostles lived; the church has no access now to apostolic content except through what was written.
The word is a lamp; its clarity is a function of God's intent to guide his people.
Christ gives teachers to the church so that believers are not tossed about; the ministry serves the reading of scripture rather than replacing it or leaving it to individuals alone.

arguments.text: Scripture alone is called theopneustos (God-breathed); no comparable claim is made in the New Testament for post-apostolic tradition or bishops.
Jesus and the apostles consistently appeal to the written scriptures as final, saying 'it is written' and 'have you not read'.
The early fathers appealed to a rule of faith that summarized scripture's content and was itself proven from scripture; this is Tradition 1, not a second source of revelation.
Councils and popes have contradicted one another (for example over Honorius I, condemned by the Third Council of Constantinople in 681), so no post-apostolic body can be guaranteed infallible.
The church's recognition of the canon is like a witness identifying a person: it does not make the person who he is. So the church is servant, not lord, of the canon.
Every authority claim, including Rome's or Orthodoxy's, must itself be interpreted and evaluated by individuals; the question is not whether people judge, but by what final standard.

critiques.text: Restorationists argue that confessional Protestants inconsistently bind conscience with subordinate standards, require ministers to subscribe to them, and in practice treat departure from the confession as heresy. That is functionally a second authority.

Catholic and Orthodox critics argue that sola scriptura is not taught in scripture, so it is self-refuting; that the New Testament canon was identified by the church's tradition; and that Protestantism's many divisions show that without an authoritative interpreter scripture's meaning cannot be secured. Christian Smith's pluralism argument is often extended to confessional Protestants as well.

The Reformers' selective use of tradition looks arbitrary: they kept Nicaea and infant baptism but rejected ancient practices such as prayers for the dead and a sacrificial understanding of the eucharist that are equally early.

responses.text: Confessional Protestants answer that confessions bind ministers by voluntary covenant, not believers' consciences before God, and that they may be revised by scripture; the Westminster Confession says synods are a help, not a rule. Mathison argues that refusing all such standards does not remove interpretive authority but hands it to each individual.

Defenders argue that scripture's sufficiency is implied by its unique inspiration and by the pattern of appeal to it; that Israel recognized the Old Testament without an infallible magisterium; and that divisions exist in Catholic and Orthodox history too. Kevin DeYoung's review of Smith argued that pluralism on secondary questions does not show the Bible is unclear on the gospel. Mathison accepts part of Smith's diagnosis but argues it applies to solo scriptura, not to sola scriptura properly understood.

Reformers reply that the test is not antiquity but agreement with scripture, applied to each practice; Calvin and Chemnitz argued in detail from the fathers that later developments departed from earlier practice.

strawMen.strawMan: Sola scriptura means 'me and my Bible' with no need for the church.
strawMen.correction: The Reformers explicitly rejected that; they held a high view of the church, the ministry and the creeds as subordinate authorities.

strawMen.strawMan: Sola scriptura means the Bible is the only source of any knowledge.
strawMen.correction: It concerns the only infallible rule of faith and practice; Reformers used reason, history, languages and the fathers freely.

strawMen.strawMan: Protestants think every passage is equally easy to understand.
strawMen.correction: Perspicuity is claimed for what is necessary for salvation, and the Westminster Confession concedes that not all things are equally plain.

positive: Made the Bible accessible in vernacular translation and preaching.
Provided a standard by which church abuses could be named and reformed.
Produced rich confessional traditions that combined exegesis with historic orthodoxy.
Encouraged literacy and education among laypeople.
negative: Did not prevent repeated Protestant schisms over interpretation.
Confessional subscription disputes have sometimes become bitter and legalistic.
Its distinction from biblicism is often lost in popular practice.
Critics see the line between subordinate and binding authority as unstable.

critic.title: Dei Verbum (Dogmatic Constitution on Divine Revelation)

positions.name: Scripture within Holy Tradition (Catholic and Orthodox)
positions.summary:
Catholic and Orthodox Christians hold that the gospel was handed on by the apostles both in writing and in the living life of the church: its worship, sacraments, creeds and teaching. Scripture is the inspired, written form of that tradition, and it is read authentically only within the church that produced, preserved and canonized it.

In Catholic teaching, Vatican II's *Dei Verbum* (1965) says that sacred tradition and sacred scripture form one sacred deposit of the word of God, flowing from the same divine wellspring, and that the task of authentically interpreting it belongs to the living teaching office (the magisterium) of the bishops in communion with the pope, which is not above the word but serves it. The Orthodox speak instead of Holy Tradition as the life of the Holy Spirit in the church, with scripture at its heart, discerned through ecumenical councils, the fathers, the liturgy and the reception of the whole people of God, without a single juridical teaching office.

figures.name: Irenaeus of Lyon
figures.bio: Against Gnostic teachers who claimed secret traditions and twisted scripture, Irenaeus appealed to the public tradition preserved in churches founded by apostles, listing bishops' successions (most famously at Rome) as guarantors that the apostolic teaching had been handed on intact. He used the 'rule of truth' as the key to reading scripture rightly.

figures.name: Vincent of Lérins
figures.bio: Vincent proposed a test for authentic doctrine: what has been believed everywhere, always and by all. He also allowed for genuine development, like a body growing, as long as the doctrine remains the same in meaning.

figures.name: Council of Trent
figures.bio: In its fourth session (1546) Trent declared that the truth and discipline of the gospel are contained in written books and in unwritten traditions received from Christ or the apostles, to be received with equal reverence, and fixed the canon including the deuterocanonical books.

figures.name: John Henry Newman
figures.bio: Newman's study of the fathers led him to argue that Christian doctrine develops organically, and that a living authority is needed to distinguish true developments from corruptions. He became Catholic in 1845, the year his *Essay* appeared.

works.author: John Henry Newman
works.title: An Essay on the Development of Christian Doctrine

figures.name: Georges Florovsky
figures.bio: Florovsky called Orthodox theology back to a 'neo-patristic synthesis'. He argued that tradition is not an added source but the Spirit-guided mind of the church, in which scripture is understood; the church is the only authentic interpreter of the book it produced.

works.author: Georges Florovsky
works.title: Bible, Church, Tradition: An Eastern Orthodox View

positions.context:
The early church had apostolic teaching before it had a New Testament. Gospels and letters circulated alongside oral instruction, liturgy and baptismal creeds. Fathers such as Irenaeus and Tertullian answered heretics who also quoted scripture by appealing to the rule of faith held in apostolic churches. The canon's boundaries were settled gradually (Athanasius' Festal Letter 39 in 367 lists the 27 New Testament books), and the great Trinitarian and Christological creeds were formulated by councils.

At the Reformation, Trent (1546) affirmed scripture and unwritten traditions together. Later Catholic theology debated whether tradition supplies content absent from scripture or interprets content materially present in it; Vatican II's *Dei Verbum* (1965) deliberately avoided settling that and stressed the unity of scripture, tradition and magisterium. Orthodoxy, which never passed through the Reformation, articulated its view in response to both Catholic and Protestant challenges, especially in the twentieth century.
claims: Divine revelation is transmitted by the apostles both in writing (scripture) and in the church's living tradition; they are not rival sources but one deposit.
Scripture is the church's book: the church produced, preserved and recognized it, and reads it rightly within its worship and faith.
The canon of scripture is itself known through tradition.
Christ promised the Spirit would guide the church into truth, so the church as a whole cannot defect from the faith.

Catholics hold that the magisterium authentically interprets the word and, under defined conditions, teaches infallibly; Orthodox locate this discernment in ecumenical councils as received by the whole church.
Genuine doctrinal development unfolds what was given once for all, without adding new revelation.

scriptures.reading: Paul commands believers to hold to the traditions taught by word of mouth or by letter; oral apostolic tradition is put on par with written.
The church, not the Bible alone, is called the pillar and foundation of the truth.
Christ builds his church on Peter and gives him the keys; the gates of Hades will not prevail, implying preserved teaching authority.
The Spirit will guide the apostles, and through them the church, into all truth, including things not yet spoken.
The council at Jerusalem settles a scriptural controversy by an authoritative decision that 'seemed good to the Holy Spirit and to us'.
Teaching is handed from apostle to faithful men who teach others, a chain of transmission.
Not everything Jesus did was written down; the church's memory exceeds the text.
The Ethiopian cannot understand Isaiah without someone to guide him; scripture needs an authorized interpreter.
Some things in Paul are hard to understand and are twisted by the ignorant; private reading is not self-sufficient.

arguments.text: The New Testament nowhere teaches that scripture alone is the rule of faith; it does command adherence to oral tradition and points to the church as the bulwark of truth.
The canon was recognized through liturgical use and episcopal and conciliar judgment over several centuries; one cannot know which books are scripture without trusting the church that discerned them.
Irenaeus and Tertullian answered heretics who quoted scripture by appealing to the tradition held in apostolic churches, which shows the early church did not operate on scripture alone.
An inspired text without an authoritative interpreter cannot settle disputes, as the multiplication of Protestant communions shows; Christ, who willed the church's unity, would have provided for it.
Doctrines all Protestants accept, such as the full Nicene Trinity and the closed canon, were defined by councils; consistent acceptance of these implies acknowledging the authority that defined them.
Christ's promises of the Spirit's guidance and of his presence to the end of the age were made to the apostolic community as a body that would continue.

critiques.text: Restorationists see in Catholic and Orthodox tradition the very 'traditions of men' Jesus condemned: doctrines and practices such as the papacy, Marian dogmas and icon veneration have no clear New Testament basis and were added over time.

Reformational critics argue that Catholic tradition has functioned as a second source introducing doctrines (for example the Immaculate Conception, 1854, and the Assumption, 1950) not found in scripture or in the earliest centuries, contradicting Vincent's own test. They add that Catholics and Orthodox disagree with each other about tradition's content (papal primacy, the filioque), so appealing to tradition does not end disagreement.
The magisterium claims to serve the word, but if it alone determines what the word means, scripture can never correct it in practice; the servant has become the master.

responses.text: Defenders distinguish apostolic Tradition from human customs; Jesus condemned traditions that nullify God's word, not tradition as such, since the apostles themselves handed on traditions. They argue that later doctrines are organic developments of what was given, as Newman argued.

Catholic theologians answer that Marian dogmas articulate what was implicit and long held in the church's worship and teaching, and that development is not addition. Orthodox and Catholics agree on far more than they disagree on, and their remaining disputes concern how tradition is discerned, not whether it exists. Christian Smith, who became Catholic, argued that interpretive pluralism is a far greater problem for Protestants than for communions with a recognized interpretive authority.

*Dei Verbum* states that the magisterium is not above the word of God but serves it, teaching only what has been handed on. Catholic theologians point to cases in which scripture study has led to genuine changes of emphasis, and Orthodox note that conciliar decisions require reception by the whole church.

strawMen.strawMan: Catholics and Orthodox put tradition above the Bible.
strawMen.correction: Both affirm scripture as inspired and uniquely authoritative; they see tradition as the context in which it is received and understood, not a superior authority.

strawMen.strawMan: Catholics are discouraged from reading the Bible.
strawMen.correction: Modern Catholic teaching, including *Dei Verbum*, urges all the faithful to read scripture frequently.

strawMen.strawMan: Tradition just means whatever the church currently does.
strawMen.correction: Both traditions distinguish apostolic Tradition from changeable customs and disciplines.

positive: Preserves continuity with the early church's worship, creeds and interpretation.
Provides a recognizable way to settle doctrinal disputes and maintain unity.
Keeps scripture tied to liturgy, prayer and community rather than private study alone.
Has produced deep traditions of patristic and spiritual interpretation.
negative: Critics argue it shields institutional errors and abuses from correction.
Dogmatic definitions have created new barriers between churches.
Disagreement between Catholic and Orthodox over authority remains unresolved.
Lay engagement with scripture has historically been uneven.

readings.reading: Scripture alone makes the believer complete; nothing else, including creeds, is needed.
Teaches the material sufficiency and unique inspiration of scripture; it does not exclude teachers or creeds as helps (Timothy himself was taught by Paul, 3:14).
Affirms scripture's inspiration and usefulness, but says nothing about scripture alone; Timothy learned it from persons within a tradition (3:14-15).
The apostles' oral teaching was the same message later written; we have it now in the New Testament.
While apostles lived, oral and written forms existed side by side; no oral content reliably traceable to them survives outside scripture.
A direct command to keep both oral and written apostolic tradition, which the church continues to transmit.
A warning against all binding religious tradition; creeds are a modern form of the elders' tradition.
Tradition must be judged by God's word; traditions that conflict with it are void, while those that agree are useful.
Condemns human customs that nullify God's commandment, not the apostolic tradition Christ himself established.
The local congregation supports the truth by holding to scripture; it is not an interpreting authority.
The church upholds and proclaims the truth ministerially; it is the truth's pillar, not its source or judge.
The church is the guarantor of revealed truth, which implies preserved teaching authority.
An apostolic, inspired decision unique to its time, not a precedent for post-apostolic councils with binding power.
A model for synods: elders deliberate from scripture and issue real but ministerial decisions.
The first council, prototype of later ecumenical councils whose decisions are Spirit-guided and binding.
Each believer checks all teaching against scripture personally.
Scripture is the final test of teaching, examined by the congregation together.
The Bereans were Jews testing whether apostolic preaching matched their scriptures; after they believed, they received the apostles' teaching as authoritative.
Some passages are hard, but the problem is the ignorant and unstable reader, not the lack of an official interpreter.
Hard texts are read with the help of clearer texts and of the church's teachers; Peter also places Paul's letters among 'the other scriptures'.
Shows that private interpretation leads to distortion and that scripture needs the church's guidance.

Believers are commanded to test teachers by scripture.

Sincere biblicists reach incompatible conclusions (pervasive interpretive pluralism).
Disagreement is mostly on secondary matters and also exists in churches with a magisterium.
Rejecting creeds simply makes each reader's private tradition the authority ('solo scriptura').

Scripture is the sole infallible rule, read within the church and its creeds.

title: Is God's justice retributive, restorative, or both?
question: When scripture calls God just and righteous, does it mean chiefly that he gives each person what they deserve, that he acts to set wrongs right and restore broken relationships, or both together, and what follows for the cross and the final judgment?
intro:
The Hebrew words mishpat and tsedaqah, and the Greek dikaiosynē, are translated 'justice' and 'righteousness'. Scripture uses them for God's judging of wrongdoers, for his rescue of the oppressed, and for his faithfulness to his covenant promises. Christians have weighted these senses differently.

A retributive account, classically developed by Anselm and the Reformers, holds that justice gives what is due: sin deserves punishment, God cannot simply overlook it, and the cross satisfies justice so that God can justly forgive. A restorative account, developed by Christopher Marshall, Howard Zehr and others and linked to N. T. Wright's reading of 'God's righteousness' as covenant faithfulness, holds that biblical justice aims above all at making things right, healing victims, offenders and communities, so that punishment, where present, serves restoration. An integrative account, associated with Miroslav Volf and Tim Keller among others, argues that scripture holds the two together: God's justice both condemns evil as it deserves and restores the world, and neither can be reduced to the other.

The answer shapes how one understands atonement (penal substitution, Christus Victor, covenant-renewal models), hell and the last judgment, and Christian engagement with criminal justice and reconciliation.

positions.name: Retributive justice
positions.summary:
On this view, God's justice is first of all his commitment to give each what is due. Because God is holy, sin is not a mere debt he could waive, but a real wrong that deserves punishment; a judge who acquits the guilty without satisfaction would be unjust. God's justice is therefore an essential attribute, not a policy.

This grounds the doctrine of penal substitution: on the cross Christ bore the penalty sinners deserved, so that God is both just and the justifier of the one who has faith in Jesus (Rom 3:26). It also grounds a final judgment in which every person is rendered according to their works and the impenitent receive the just penalty of sin. Proponents insist that retribution is not revenge: it is measured, impartial and rooted in the moral order God's own character establishes, and it affirms human dignity by treating people as responsible agents.

figures.name: Anselm of Canterbury
figures.bio: In *Cur Deus Homo* Anselm argued that sin robs God of the honor due to him, that God's justice does not allow sin to go unpunished or unrepaid, and that only one who is both God and human could make the necessary satisfaction. Strictly his model is satisfaction rather than punishment, but it set the frame for later retributive accounts.

works.author: Anselm
works.title: Cur Deus Homo (Why God Became Man)

figures.name: John Calvin
figures.bio: Calvin taught that Christ took the place of sinners before God's judgment seat, bearing the curse and wrath that their sins deserved, so that the righteous anger of God was appeased and his justice satisfied. He insisted that God's love preceded and motivated this, not the reverse.

figures.name: Charles Hodge
figures.bio: Hodge distinguished God's rectoral justice from his distributive justice and argued that punitive justice is essential to God, so that the punishment of sin is not merely useful for deterrence or reform but required by God's own nature.

figures.name: Leon Morris
figures.bio: Morris argued against C. H. Dodd that hilastērion and related words in the New Testament carry the sense of propitiation, the turning away of God's personal, just wrath, and that justification is forensic.

works.author: Leon Morris
works.title: The Apostolic Preaching of the Cross

works.title: The Cross in the New Testament

figures.name: J. I. Packer
figures.bio: Packer's 1973 Tyndale Biblical Theology Lecture (published 1974) defended penal substitution as the heart of the gospel, presenting retribution as God's just response to sin and the cross as God himself bearing it in love.

works.author: J. I. Packer
works.title: What Did the Cross Achieve? The Logic of Penal Substitution (Tyndale Bulletin 25)

positions.context:
Patristic writers used many images for the atonement: ransom, victory, sacrifice, healing. Anselm's 1098 treatise gave the first systematic argument that God's justice requires satisfaction for sin. The Reformers, trained in law and reading Paul's forensic language of justification, recast satisfaction as the bearing of penalty. Protestant scholastics and later Princeton theologians held retributive justice to be essential to God.

In the twentieth century the view was challenged by liberal theologians, by C. H. Dodd's reading of hilastērion as expiation, and later by feminist and nonviolent critics who saw it as divine violence. Evangelical defenders such as Morris, Packer and later John Stott (*The Cross of Christ*, 1986) restated it. In ethics, retributivism is also a major philosophical theory of punishment, defended in different forms by Kant and by many modern legal theorists.
claims: Justice is giving each what is due, and God is perfectly just in this sense by nature.
Sin is a real offense against God that deserves punishment; God cannot ignore it without contradicting himself.
On the cross Christ bore the penalty of sin in the place of sinners, satisfying God's justice.
Through this substitution God remains just while justifying the ungodly who believe.
At the final judgment each person will be repaid according to deeds, and the impenitent will justly suffer the penalty of sin.
Retribution differs from vengeance: it is proportionate, impartial and grounded in moral truth.
Treating wrongdoers as deserving punishment respects them as responsible moral agents.

scriptures.reading: God will render to each according to his works; reward and penalty correspond to desert.
God put Christ forward as a propitiation to demonstrate his righteousness, because he had passed over former sins; the cross shows he is just in justifying believers.
The angel praises God as just in his judgments because those who shed the blood of saints receive what they deserve.
Abraham assumes that the Judge of all the earth will not treat the righteous and the wicked alike; justice distinguishes desert.
God is merciful and forgiving, yet will by no means clear the guilty; mercy does not cancel justice.
It is just for God to repay with affliction those who afflict his people, with eternal destruction at Christ's return.
The servant is pierced for our transgressions; the LORD laid on him the iniquity of us all, the punishment that brought us peace.
The wages of sin is death: penalty is what sin earns.
Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us, a substitution in judgment.

arguments.text: Paul explains the cross as solving a problem of divine justice: God had passed over sins, and the cross shows his righteousness so that he can be just and justifier.
The language of wages, recompense and repayment saturates biblical teaching on judgment, which presupposes desert.
Old Testament sacrifice and the suffering servant present a substitute bearing the consequences due to others.
If punishment is justified only by its results (reform, deterrence, restoration), one could justly punish the innocent if it produced good results; only desert explains why that is unjust.
Forgiveness is meaningful only if wrong genuinely deserves condemnation; a God who did not take desert seriously would make forgiveness trivial.
From Anselm through the Reformers and the Protestant confessions, the satisfaction of divine justice has been a central way the Western church has explained the cross.

critiques.text: Christopher Marshall and others argue that this view imports Western legal and feudal categories into scripture, reducing the rich covenantal sense of tsedaqah to a cold principle of desert. It makes God seem bound by an abstract law above himself and pictures the Father punishing the Son, which critics say obscures the Trinity's united love.

Biblical justice language most often describes God rescuing the oppressed and vindicating the needy, not inflicting penalties; retributive accounts sideline this and have historically sat comfortably with harsh penal systems.

Integrative critics agree that God punishes evil but argue that a purely retributive account treats the final goal of justice as balancing accounts rather than the renewal of creation, and can neglect the Bible's call for justice for the poor.

responses.text: Defenders reply that God's justice is not a law above him but his own holy character, and that Calvin and Stott stress that the Father gives the Son and the Son gives himself in one act of Trinitarian love. Forensic language is Paul's own (justify, condemn, judgment seat), not a medieval import.

Retributivists accept that God defends the oppressed, but note that defending victims necessarily involves judging oppressors; the same psalms that celebrate rescue celebrate judgment. Retributive theory also limits punishment to what is deserved, which can restrain harsh penal systems.

Most defenders do not claim retribution is the whole of God's purpose; they claim it is a non-negotiable element that grounds atonement and judgment, and they support mercy ministries as an outworking of God's character.

strawMen.strawMan: Retributive justice is just divine revenge or anger management.
strawMen.correction: Defenders define it as proportionate, impartial recompense rooted in God's holy character, not personal vindictiveness.

strawMen.strawMan: Penal substitution pits a wrathful Father against a loving Son.
strawMen.correction: Its classic defenders insist the Father and Son act together in love, and that God himself bears the penalty in Christ.

strawMen.strawMan: Retributivists care only about punishment and ignore social justice.
strawMen.correction: Many, such as Calvin and later evangelical social reformers, held retributive views alongside strong concern for the poor.

positive: Takes the seriousness of sin and the moral responsibility of persons with full weight.
Gives a clear account of why the cross was necessary and how forgiveness is just.
Assures victims that wrongs will not ultimately be ignored.
Provides grounds for proportionality and limits on punishment.
negative: Has been used to justify harsh or vengeful penal practices.
Can present God's love as secondary to or conditional on justice in popular preaching.
May neglect the restorative and social dimensions of biblical justice.
Some find its picture of the atonement morally troubling.

adherents: Most conservative evangelical and Baptist churches
Classical Thomist accounts of punishment (in modified form)

proponent.title: Pierced for Our Transgressions

critic.title: Recovering the Scandal of the Cross

positions.name: Restorative justice
positions.summary:
On this view, the core biblical meaning of justice is making things right. Tsedaqah and mishpat describe God's saving action to restore right relationships between himself, people and creation, especially by rescuing the weak and oppressed. God's righteousness in Paul is his covenant faithfulness, his commitment to put the world to rights through Israel's Messiah.

Punishment is not denied, but it is understood as serving a restorative end or as the consequence of persistent refusal of restoration, rather than as the essence of justice. The cross is God's act of solidarity, victory and covenant renewal that overcomes sin and reconciles enemies; final judgment is God's setting of all things right. Christopher Marshall argued in *Beyond Retribution* (2001) that the New Testament vision of justice is fundamentally restorative and should shape Christian approaches to crime and punishment, joining the restorative justice movement associated with Howard Zehr.

figures.name: Howard Zehr
figures.bio: Often called a grandfather of the modern restorative justice movement. Drawing on Mennonite victim-offender reconciliation programs begun in the 1970s, he argued that crime is chiefly a violation of people and relationships, and that justice should seek to repair harm rather than primarily inflict pain.

works.title: Changing Lenses: A New Focus for Crime and Justice

works.title: The Little Book of Restorative Justice

figures.name: Christopher D. Marshall
figures.profession: New Zealand New Testament scholar, Victoria University of Wellington
figures.bio: Marshall argued from the New Testament that God's justice is primarily saving and restorative, that Jesus' teaching on forgiveness and the cross redefine justice, and that punishment should serve the restoration of relationships. He does not deny judgment, but argues that retribution is not its final or controlling purpose.

works.author: Christopher D. Marshall
works.title: Beyond Retribution: A New Testament Vision for Justice, Crime, and Punishment

works.author: Christopher D. Marshall
works.title: The Little Book of Biblical Justice

figures.name: N. T. Wright
figures.profession: Anglican bishop and New Testament scholar
figures.bio: Wright reads 'the righteousness of God' in Romans as God's covenant faithfulness, through which he deals with sin and puts the world to rights. He sees final judgment as the moment of cosmic setting-right. Wright himself retains a place for penal substitution within a larger narrative of vocation and victory, so he supports the restorative frame without rejecting all penal language.

works.author: N. T. Wright
works.title: Evil and the Justice of God

figures.name: Desmond Tutu
figures.bio: As chair of South Africa's Truth and Reconciliation Commission, Tutu advocated restorative justice grounded in Christian forgiveness and the African concept of ubuntu, arguing that healing a society required truth-telling and reconciliation rather than only punishment.

positions.context:
In 1899 the German scholar Hermann Cremer argued that biblical righteousness is a relational concept, the fulfilment of the claims of a relationship, rather than conformity to an abstract norm. This view shaped much twentieth-century biblical theology and Paul scholarship, including the 'new perspective' readings of the righteousness of God.

In parallel, Mennonites in Kitchener, Ontario, began victim-offender reconciliation in 1974, and the restorative justice movement grew in criminology through the 1980s and 1990s. Christian theologians, many from Anabaptist or peace-church traditions, brought these streams together, critiquing penal substitution and retributive criminal justice as mutually reinforcing. South Africa's Truth and Reconciliation Commission (from 1995) gave the ideas global visibility.
claims: Biblical justice is primarily relational: God acting to make right what is wrong and to restore right relationships.
God's justice is especially displayed in rescuing the poor, the oppressed and the stranger.
The 'righteousness of God' in Paul refers to God's covenant faithfulness and saving action, not first to a standard of desert.
Punishment, where present, serves restoration or names the consequence of refusing it; it is not the goal of justice.
The cross is God's act of reconciliation and victory over sin and evil, and can be understood without making retribution its center.
Final judgment is God's setting the whole creation right.
Christians should favor restorative practices in criminal justice that address harm to victims and communities.

scriptures.reading: The servant brings forth justice gently, not breaking a bruised reed; justice is the establishment of a healed order.
Jesus' mission statement defines his work as release, healing and good news to the poor, drawing on jubilee: justice as liberation and restoration.
What the LORD requires is doing justice, loving kindness and walking humbly; justice is paired with covenant love (hesed), not opposed to it.
The righteousness of God is revealed as his covenant faithfulness, putting things right through the faithfulness of Jesus the Messiah, for Jew and Gentile alike.
The God who executes justice feeds the hungry, frees prisoners and upholds orphans and widows.
The anointed one proclaims liberty and comfort and rebuilds ruins: justice as repair.
Through the cross God reconciles all things to himself, making peace; the goal is restoration.
Believers overcome evil with good and leave wrath to God; the community's response to wrong is restorative.
Church discipline aims at regaining the brother, a restorative process.

arguments.text: In the prophets and psalms, God's justice is most often described as rescuing, defending and restoring the vulnerable.
Jesus' table fellowship with sinners and his teaching on forgiveness show a justice that seeks the restoration of the offender.
Romans 1-4 is about God being faithful to his covenant promise to Abraham to bless the nations; 'righteousness' there is a saving activity.
Biblical-theological research since Cremer has widely recognized tsedaqah as relational and covenantal rather than a strictly forensic norm.
Punishment that leaves victims unhealed and offenders unchanged leaves the world no more just; real justice must aim at repairing harm.
Restorative practices from victim-offender mediation to truth commissions have shown measurable benefits for victims and communities, which is consistent with a biblical vision of shalom.

critiques.text: Retributivists argue that this view cannot account for the many texts that speak of wrath, repayment and eternal punishment, or for Paul's language of propitiation in Romans 3:25. If justice is only restoration, the final judgment of the impenitent becomes unintelligible or is quietly dropped.

Making restoration the essence of justice detaches punishment from desert; if punishment is justified only by good outcomes, nothing in principle forbids punishing the innocent or over-punishing the guilty for social benefit.

Volf and others argue that restoration and reconciliation presuppose a truthful judgment that wrong is wrong; forgiveness without the naming of desert can trivialize victims' suffering. Victims in scripture cry out for vindication, not only for healing.

responses.text: Marshall and Wright do not deny wrath or judgment. Wrath is God's settled opposition to what destroys his creatures and often takes the form of handing people over to the consequences of their choices; final judgment is the exclusion of what refuses to be restored. Hilastērion can be read as the mercy seat, the place where God deals with sin, without importing retributive theory.

Restorative theorists affirm that punishment must be proportionate and that the innocent must not be harmed, because restoring right relationship requires truthful accountability. Accountability is central to restorative processes, not absent from them.

Restorative justice begins with naming the harm and hearing victims; truth-telling is its first step. Advocates agree that reconciliation without truth is cheap, which is why truth commissions required public disclosure.

strawMen.strawMan: Restorative justice means God never judges or punishes anyone.
strawMen.correction: Most proponents affirm divine judgment and real consequences; they dispute that retribution is its essence or final aim.

strawMen.strawMan: Restorative theologians all reject substitution.
strawMen.correction: Some do, but others, including N. T. Wright, keep substitution within a broader restorative and covenantal framework.

strawMen.strawMan: Restorative justice is soft on crime and ignores victims.
strawMen.correction: The movement originated in concern that criminal justice sidelined victims; it centers their voices and requires offenders to take responsibility.

positive: Recovered the prominence of the poor and oppressed in biblical justice.
Shaped humane reforms such as victim-offender mediation and truth commissions.
Connects atonement to reconciliation, community and the renewal of creation.
Encourages churches to practice discipline aimed at restoration.
negative: Can underplay texts on wrath, desert and final judgment.
Some forms dissolve the necessity of the cross into an example of love.
Its criminological claims are sometimes stretched beyond what evidence supports.
May leave unclear what happens to the finally impenitent.

adherents: Proponents of the new perspective on Paul (in varying degrees)
Christian restorative justice organizations and prison ministries

proponent.title: Evil and the Justice of God

critic.title: The Apostolic Preaching of the Cross

critic.author: Steve Jeffery, Michael Ovey, Andrew Sach
critic.title: Pierced for Our Transgressions

positions.name: Integrative: retributive and restorative
positions.summary:
Integrative accounts argue that both of the other views capture something scripture holds together. God's justice gives what is due, condemning and punishing evil, and it also rescues, heals and sets right. These are not two competing justices but aspects of one: God judges evil precisely because he is committed to restoring his creation, and he restores it in a way that does not pretend evil was acceptable.

Tim Keller, in *Generous Justice* (2010), distinguishes 'rectifying justice' (punishing wrongdoers and caring for victims) from 'primary justice' (right relationships of generosity and care) and grounds both in the character of God. Miroslav Volf, writing out of the Balkan wars, argued in *Exclusion and Embrace* (1996) that the embrace of enemies requires a God who will finally judge: the hope that God will judge justly is what allows victims to renounce vengeance. On the cross, God both bears the judgment due to sin and reconciles enemies; at the last judgment, he both condemns what is evil and makes all things new.

figures.name: Miroslav Volf
figures.bio: Volf's work on reconciliation, forged in the context of war in the former Yugoslavia, argues that embrace of the other cannot bypass truth and justice, and that belief in God's final judgment is a precondition for nonviolence rather than its enemy. He also stresses that the cross is God's self-giving love that makes room for the enemy.

figures.name: Timothy Keller
figures.profession: Presbyterian pastor, founder of Redeemer Presbyterian Church, New York
figures.bio: Keller combined a firm defense of penal substitution and final judgment with a strong emphasis on justice for the poor, arguing that the gospel of grace motivates generous justice and that biblical mishpat includes both punishing wrongdoing and giving people their rights.

figures.name: Nicholas Wolterstorff
figures.bio: Wolterstorff grounds justice in inherent rights and argues that love and justice are not opposed. In *Justice in Love* he treats forgiveness as the forgoing of retributive punishment that is otherwise just, while arguing that much in the New Testament reframes rather than abolishes retribution.

figures.name: Fleming Rutledge
figures.bio: Rutledge's study of the crucifixion argues that the New Testament uses many motifs, including substitution, victory and sacrifice, and that God's righteousness is best understood as rectification: God making right what is wrong, which includes judgment on sin and the powers.

works.author: Fleming Rutledge
works.title: The Crucifixion: Understanding the Death of Jesus Christ

positions.context:
Integrative positions emerged in conversation with both older penal accounts and the restorative and nonviolent critiques of the late twentieth century. Volf wrote amid ethnic cleansing in his homeland and asked how a victim could forgive without denying justice. Keller ministered in a secular city where both judgment and justice for the poor were contested topics. Philosophers such as Wolterstorff reopened the question of whether love and justice compete.

In atonement theology, the integrative impulse appears in multi-model accounts that place penal substitution within Christus Victor and reconciliation frameworks (for example in the 2006 collection *The Nature of the Atonement: Four Views*), and in apocalyptic readings of Paul that speak of rectification.
claims: God's justice includes both rendering what is deserved and setting wrongs right; neither is reducible to the other.
Judgment and restoration serve one purpose: the renewal of a creation in which evil has no place.
The cross both bears judgment on sin and accomplishes reconciliation and victory.
Final judgment is good news for victims because it guarantees that wrongs will be named and redressed.
Belief in God's just judgment frees humans to renounce personal vengeance and pursue reconciliation.
Biblical mishpat includes both punishing wrongdoing and giving people their due rights and care.
Mercy does not abolish justice but fulfils it at God's own cost.

scriptures.reading: Steadfast love and faithfulness meet; righteousness and peace kiss; the two are united rather than opposed.
The LORD waits to be gracious, for he is a God of justice: his justice is the ground of his grace.
God's righteousness is both his saving faithfulness (3:21-22) and his just dealing with sin through propitiation (3:25-26).
Believers leave vengeance to God precisely because he will repay, and so are free to feed their enemies.
Creation rejoices that the LORD comes to judge; judgment is the setting right of the world.
God wipes away tears and makes all things new, while excluding what is evil (21:8): restoration and judgment together.
The Messiah judges the poor with righteousness and strikes the earth with the rod of his mouth: rescue and judgment in one rule.
God has fixed a day to judge the world in righteousness by the man he appointed, which grounds the call to repent.

arguments.text: Many texts place judgment and salvation side by side as two faces of God's one coming to set the world right.
Romans 3 uses righteousness both for God's saving faithfulness and for his just dealing with sin; reading only one sense flattens the passage.
Forgiveness presupposes that wrong has been truthfully judged; restoration that bypasses desert is not forgiveness but denial.
Volf's argument: when victims believe God will justly judge, they are released from the need to avenge themselves; removing divine judgment tends to increase human violence rather than decrease it.
The church fathers used both penal and restorative images of the cross without felt contradiction; separating them is a modern development.
Christian social movements such as abolition were often led by people who held strong views of divine judgment and also pursued restorative social justice.

critiques.text: Retributivists worry that integrative accounts blur categories, making retribution one option among others instead of the necessary ground of atonement. Without a clear priority, they fear the necessity of penal substitution and of final punishment will erode.

Restorative critics argue that keeping retribution as part of God's justice keeps the problem they identified: a God whose justice still finally requires suffering in proportion to guilt. They question whether Volf's argument from human violence is consistent with Jesus' call to love enemies as God does.
Critics argue that 'both-and' language can function rhetorically to keep a penal core while adopting the vocabulary of social justice, without showing how the two cohere.

responses.text: Integrative theologians such as Keller fully affirm penal substitution and final judgment; they situate them within God's broader purpose rather than weakening them. The question is about priority and goal, not about denying retribution.

Volf argues that loving enemies is possible for humans precisely because God, not they, holds the right to judge; Jesus' teaching on enemy-love sits in the same Sermon as warnings of judgment. God's perfect judgment differs from human vengeance in knowledge and impartiality.

Defenders point to specific accounts of coherence: Rutledge's rectification theme, Keller's distinction of rectifying and primary justice, and Wolterstorff's treatment of forgiveness as forgoing just punishment for the sake of reconciliation.

strawMen.strawMan: Integrative views are just a vague compromise that avoids taking a side.
strawMen.correction: Its leading proponents make specific arguments about how judgment serves restoration and about how forgiveness presupposes desert.

strawMen.strawMan: Volf endorses violence in God's name.
strawMen.correction: Volf argues the opposite: trust in God's judgment is what allows humans to renounce violence.

strawMen.strawMan: Keller's emphasis on justice for the poor means he abandoned substitutionary atonement.
strawMen.correction: Keller consistently defended penal substitution and grounded social concern in it.

positive: Holds together evangelical atonement theology and concern for justice in society.
Offers a theology of forgiveness that takes victims' suffering seriously.
Gives a coherent hope that the last judgment will both condemn evil and heal creation.
Has influenced reconciliation work in post-conflict societies.
negative: The relation between the two aspects remains disputed and sometimes underdeveloped.
Critics on both sides see it as unstable.
Popular use can reduce it to slogans.
Does not resolve disputes over the nature of hell.

adherents: Some Catholic social thought (justice and mercy united)

readings.reading: Propitiation satisfies God's justice so that he can justify sinners without compromising it.
The mercy seat is where God deals with sin in covenant faithfulness; 'righteousness' is his saving action, not a retributive standard.
Both: God shows saving faithfulness and also deals justly with sin; the passage resists reduction to either.
A plain statement of retributive principle at the final judgment.
Judgment according to works shows that God's verdict matches the reality of a life; its aim is the vindication of those who seek glory and the end of evil.
Retribution is real, and it serves God's purpose of setting the world right.
Describes human ethical duty; God's own justice includes punishing sin, as Micah's judgment oracles show.
Justice paired with hesed shows justice is relational faithfulness and care, not cold desert.
Justice and steadfast love are inseparable, as in God's own character.
The servant establishes a just order on earth, which elsewhere includes judgment on the nations.
The servant's justice is gentle and healing, not breaking the bruised reed: the model of restorative justice.
The servant brings forth justice faithfully, combining care for the weak with a just order for the nations.
God's judgments are praised as just because they are deserved.
Apocalyptic imagery of evil receiving its own violence back; the goal is the end of oppression and a new creation.
Judgment on oppressors is vindication of victims and part of the way to the new creation of chapter 21.
Jesus announces the year of the LORD's favor, notably stopping before Isaiah's 'day of vengeance', which is postponed rather than cancelled.
Jesus defines his mission as release and healing; his omission of vengeance is deliberate and revealing.
The present age is one of favor and restoration; judgment remains for the end, as Jesus' later teaching shows.
God will repay; retribution belongs to him and to the state (13:4), not to private persons.
Believers renounce vengeance and overcome evil with good; this reflects God's own restorative way.
Trust in God's repayment is exactly what frees believers to love enemies, as Volf argues.

title: Can a true believer lose salvation?
question: Once a person has genuinely come to saving faith in Christ, is their final salvation certain, or can it be forfeited, and if so how, and can it be regained?
intro:
The New Testament contains strong assurances that Christ will keep those the Father gives him, and also sharp warnings that some who have tasted the heavenly gift may fall away. Every tradition must account for both kinds of text, and each does so differently.

The Reformed doctrine of the perseverance of the saints (Synod of Dort, 1619; Westminster Confession chapter 17) holds that all whom God has truly regenerated will persevere in faith to the end, kept by God; those who finally fall away were never truly regenerate. The Arminian and Wesleyan doctrine of conditional security holds that believers are secure while they remain in Christ by faith, but can genuinely abandon faith and be lost. The Free Grace view, a strand of popular once-saved-always-saved teaching shaped by Zane Hodges and Charles Ryrie, holds that anyone who has once believed is eternally saved regardless of later fruit or even continued belief, with the warnings referring to rewards, discipline or discipleship. Catholic and Orthodox churches teach that grace received in baptism can be lost by grave (mortal) sin and restored through repentance and, in Catholic teaching, the sacrament of penance; final perseverance is a gift no one can presume.

The debate concerns not only the warnings but assurance, the nature of saving faith, the relationship between justification and sanctification, and the pastoral care of those who drift.

positions.name: Perseverance of the saints (Reformed)
positions.summary:
In Reformed theology, God's saving work is a single chain from election to glorification. Those whom God effectually calls and regenerates he also keeps; they may fall into serious sin for a time, grieve the Spirit and lose the felt assurance of salvation, but they cannot totally or finally fall from grace. Their perseverance depends not on their own free will but on the unchangeable election of the Father, the merit and intercession of Christ, the indwelling Spirit and the nature of the covenant of grace.

The warning passages are real and addressed to real people. Reformed theologians typically read them either as describing people who professed faith and experienced the church's blessings without being regenerate (1 John 2:19), or as the very means God uses to keep his elect persevering (Schreiner and Caneday). Perseverance is therefore not passivity: true believers persevere because God works in them to will and to work.

figures.name: Augustine of Hippo
figures.bio: Augustine taught that final perseverance is a distinct gift of God given to the elect. He also held, unlike later Reformed theology, that some who were truly baptized and regenerated did not receive this gift and fell away, so he is a precursor of the doctrine rather than its exact source.

figures.name: Synod of Dort
figures.bio: Convened to answer the Remonstrants, the synod's Fifth Head of Doctrine teaches that God preserves the regenerate so that, though they may fall into grievous sins, they do not totally lose faith and grace; it also treats assurance and the use of warnings and means.

figures.name: John Owen
figures.profession: English Puritan theologian, Vice-Chancellor of Oxford
figures.bio: Owen wrote a massive defense of perseverance against the Arminian John Goodwin's *Redemption Redeemed* (1651), grounding it in God's immutability, the covenant, Christ's intercession and the Spirit's indwelling.

figures.name: Westminster Assembly
figures.profession: Assembly of English and Scottish divines

figures.name: Thomas R. Schreiner

figures.bio: With Ardel Caneday, Schreiner argued that the warnings are prospective, conditional means by which God preserves his people: they genuinely threaten eternal loss to those who fall away, and God uses them to ensure that the elect do not.

positions.context:
Augustine's controversy with Pelagians and with monks in Gaul produced the first developed doctrine of the gift of perseverance. The Reformers, especially Calvin, linked it to election and to Christ's intercession, and taught that true faith, though it may be weakened, is never extinguished.

The doctrine was formalized in response to the Remonstrants, whose 1610 articles left open whether believers could fall away. Dort (1619) made perseverance the fifth of its heads of doctrine, the 'P' of the later TULIP acronym. English Puritans and the Westminster Assembly adopted it, and it remains the standard teaching of Reformed, Presbyterian and Reformed Baptist churches. In the twentieth century it was distinguished from the popular once-saved-always-saved teaching by its insistence that true faith perseveres in holiness.
claims: All whom God has effectually called and regenerated will persevere in faith and be finally saved.
Perseverance depends on God's unchangeable election, Christ's merit and intercession, and the indwelling Spirit, not on human free will.
True believers may fall into grievous sin and lose assurance for a time, but never totally or finally fall from grace.
Those who finally abandon the faith show that they were never truly regenerate.
Warning passages are genuine and are means God uses to preserve his people.
Perseverance in faith and holiness is the necessary evidence of genuine faith.
Believers may attain a well-founded assurance of salvation in this life.

scriptures.reading: Christ gives eternal life to his sheep; they will never perish, and no one can snatch them from his or the Father's hand.
God who began a good work will bring it to completion at the day of Christ; what he starts he finishes.
Nothing in all creation, which includes the believer's own future, can separate believers from God's love in Christ.
Those foreknown, predestined, called and justified are glorified; no link in the chain is lost.
Jesus will lose none of those the Father gives him but will raise them up at the last day.
Those who went out showed they were never of us; had they been, they would have continued.
Believers are guarded by God's power through faith for a salvation ready to be revealed.
The Spirit is the seal and guarantee of the inheritance until it is acquired.
God is able to keep believers from stumbling and present them blameless.

arguments.text: Jesus explicitly promises that his sheep will never perish and cannot be taken from the Father's hand.
Paul's golden chain links predestination and calling inseparably to glorification.
John explains apostasy as revealing that those who left were never truly part of the community.
If salvation ultimately depends on the believer's continued free choice, then it rests finally on human performance, which conflicts with salvation by grace alone.
Christ's intercession is always effective; he prays that his own will be kept, and the Father always hears him.
From Augustine through Dort and Westminster, the Western church's most extended reflection on grace has affirmed that final perseverance is God's gift to the elect.

critiques.text: Arminian critics argue that the doctrine empties the warnings of real force: if those warned cannot fall away, the warnings address a hypothetical, and the 'never truly saved' explanation does not fit descriptions such as 'once enlightened, tasted the heavenly gift, shared in the Holy Spirit' (Heb 6:4) or 'sanctified by the blood of the covenant' (Heb 10:29).

Free Grace critics argue that Reformed perseverance actually undermines assurance: if only those who persevere in holiness were truly saved, no one can be sure of salvation until death, and assurance is drawn from one's works rather than from Christ's promise.

Catholic and Orthodox critics argue that the doctrine is a novelty against the early church, which consistently taught that the baptized could fall through grave sin and be restored by repentance, and that even Augustine allowed regenerate persons to fall away. Trent condemned claims of certain knowledge of final perseverance without special revelation.

responses.text: Reformed exegetes argue that Hebrews 6 describes covenant privileges that apostates genuinely experienced without regeneration (compare Israel in the wilderness), and that 6:9 distinguishes the readers from them. Schreiner and Caneday add that warnings are not hypothetical but are God's appointed means: they truly state that apostates perish, and through them God keeps the elect from apostasy.

Reformed theology grounds assurance first in Christ's promises, secondarily in the Spirit's inward witness and the evidence of grace, as Westminster 18 explains. The fruit is evidence of faith, not its ground, and assurance can be real though not perfect.

Reformed theologians reply that scripture, not later tradition, is decisive, and that the early church was not uniform on this point. They distinguish the visible baptized community, from which many fall, from the elect regenerate, who do not.

strawMen.strawMan: Perseverance means you can live however you like once saved.
strawMen.correction: That is a popular version of once-saved-always-saved. Reformed perseverance teaches that true believers will persevere in faith and holiness; persistent unrepentant sin calls profession into question.

strawMen.strawMan: Calvinists think believers never fall into serious sin.
strawMen.correction: Dort and Westminster explicitly say the regenerate may fall into grievous sins for a time.

strawMen.strawMan: Reformed theology treats warnings as meaningless.
strawMen.correction: Reformed exegetes take warnings as real and as instruments God uses to preserve his people.

positive: Grounds assurance in God's faithfulness rather than in human resolve.
Links genuine faith to a life of growing holiness.
Gives struggling believers hope that God will finish his work.
Produced a rich Puritan literature on assurance and spiritual counsel.
negative: Introspective believers can struggle to know whether their faith is genuine.
The 'never truly saved' explanation can feel unfalsifiable to critics.
Popular confusion with once-saved-always-saved can encourage complacency.
Can produce harsh judgments about those who drift from church.

adherents: Many Southern Baptists and other Calvinistic evangelicals

positions.name: Conditional security (Arminian and Wesleyan)
positions.summary:
Conditional security holds that believers are fully secure in Christ while they continue in faith, and that no external power can snatch them away, but that a believer can freely turn away from Christ in persistent unbelief and so be lost. Salvation is not earned by perseverance, but it is received and kept through faith, and faith is a living relationship that can be abandoned.

The warnings of Hebrews, Jesus' vine-and-branches teaching and Peter's description of those who escape the world's defilements and then return to it are read at face value as describing genuine believers. Wesleyans add that sin can wound and, if persisted in, destroy the believer's relationship with God, but that God graciously restores the repentant. Some Reformed Arminians (for example many Free Will Baptists) hold that apostasy occurs only through unbelief, not through sin as such, and is irreversible, following Hebrews 6.

figures.name: Jacobus Arminius
figures.profession: Dutch Reformed theologian, professor at Leiden
figures.bio: Arminius questioned unconditional election and taught that grace is resistible. On perseverance he was cautious: in his 1608 *Declaration of Sentiments* he said he had never taught that a true believer can totally or finally fall away, yet that some scriptures seemed to point that way and deserved careful study.

figures.name: The Remonstrants (Simon Episcopius)
figures.bio: The 1610 Remonstrance left the question of falling away open for further study. By the time of Dort, the Remonstrants' statement of opinions (1618), associated with Episcopius, affirmed that true believers can fall from faith and be finally lost.

figures.name: John Wesley
figures.bio: Wesley argued that a believer can make shipwreck of faith and perish, citing the warnings and examples of apostasy, while also stressing God's prevenient and sustaining grace and the possibility of restoration for backsliders.

works.author: John Wesley
works.title: Serious Thoughts upon the Perseverance of the Saints

figures.name: Robert Shank
figures.bio: Shank, a Baptist who had held eternal security, became convinced through study of the New Testament that perseverance is conditional on continuing faith. His book, written for a Baptist audience, became a standard modern defense of conditional security.

works.author: Robert Shank
works.title: Life in the Son: A Study of the Doctrine of Perseverance

figures.profession: New Testament scholar, University of Aberdeen
figures.bio: Marshall surveyed the New Testament evidence on falling away and argued that the possibility of real apostasy is taught, while stressing God's keeping power and the believer's assurance through ongoing faith.
